document: Arduino Language Reference: int / millis()
revision: arduino/reference-en master, last commit b367b025a1 (2025-04-11); rendered at docs.arduino.cc/language-reference
section: Variables > Data Types > int; Functions > Time > millis() (Notes and Warnings)
verbatim_snippet: On the Arduino Uno (and other ATmega based boards) an int stores a 16-bit (2-byte) value. This yields a range of -32,768 to 32,767 (minimum value of -2^15 and a maximum value of (2^15) - 1). [millis():] The return value for millis() is of type `unsigned long`, logic errors may occur if a programmer tries to do arithmetic with smaller data types such as `int`.
notes: Two passages from two reference pages (int.adoc line 18; millis.adoc line 68). The page does not literally say 'store it in an unsigned long'; it warns about arithmetic with smaller types. HTML doc: page=null.

document: Using the GNU Compiler Collection (GCC): Options to Request or Suppress Warnings
section: 3.8 Options to Request or Suppress Warnings: -Wfatal-errors
verbatim_snippet: This option causes the compiler to abort compilation on the first error occurred rather than trying to keep going and printing further error messages.
notes: No GCC/ld manual passage states that later errors are consequences of the first or advises fixing the first error first. Closest official text implies the compiler keeps going after an error and prints further messages. The current snippet's 'fix the first error and rebuild' advice is not in the source; treat as a weak/indirect citation.

document: Using the GNU Compiler Collection (GCC): Options for Code Generation Conventions
section: 3.17 Options for Code Generation Conventions: -fno-common
verbatim_snippet: The default is -fno-common, which specifies that the compiler places uninitialized global variables in the BSS section of the object file. This inhibits the merging of tentative definitions by the linker so you get a multiple-definition error if the same variable is accidentally defined in more than one compilation unit.
notes: Supports the multiple-definition link error, but GCC docs do not contain the 'define in header / declare extern in header and define in one source file' remedy verbatim (the same paragraph only mentions 'declarations of a variable with the extern keyword, which do not allocate storage'). Note the default is -fno-common since GCC 10; older AVR-GCC toolchains defaulted to -fcommon, under which uninitialized tentative definitions would NOT error — relevant if the case variable is uninitialized.

document: MPU-6000 and MPU-6050 Product Specification (PS-MPU-6000A-00)
section: 9.2 I2C Interface
verbatim_snippet: The slave address of the MPU-60X0 is b110100X which is 7 bits long. The LSB bit of the 7 bit address is determined by the logic level on pin AD0. This allows two MPU-60X0s to be connected to the same I2C bus. When used in this configuration, the address of the one of the devices should be b1101000 (pin AD0 is logic low) and the address of the other should be b1101001 (pin AD0 is logic high).
notes: Official TDK/InvenSense URL (Rev 3.4, invensense.tdk.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/02/MPU-6000-Datasheet1.pdf) returned HTML twice; verified against SparkFun mirror of Rev 3.1. Source gives binary b1101000/b1101001, not hex 0x68/0x69 (the current snippet's hex values are a derived hint). Printed '36 of 57'.

document: ESP-IDF Programming Guide: Fatal Errors
section: Guru Meditation Errors > LoadProhibited, StoreProhibited
verbatim_snippet: These CPU exceptions happen when an application attempts to read from or write to an invalid memory location. The address which has been written/read is found in the ``EXCVADDR`` register in the register dump. If this address is zero, it usually means that the application has attempted to dereference a NULL pointer.
notes: Next sentence: 'If this address is close to zero, it usually means that the application has attempted to access a member of a structure, but the pointer to the structure is NULL.' (current snippet merges the two).

document: ESP-IDF Programming Guide: Watchdogs
section: Watchdogs > Task Watchdog Timer (TWDT)
verbatim_snippet: The Task Watchdog Timer (TWDT) is used to monitor particular tasks, ensuring that they are able to execute within a given timeout period. The TWDT primarily watches the Idle Tasks of each CPU, however any task can subscribe to be watched by the TWDT. By watching the Idle Tasks of each CPU, the TWDT can detect instances of tasks running for a prolonged period of time wihtout yielding.
notes: 'Idle Tasks of each CPU' is the ESP32 substitution of {IDF_TARGET_IDLE_TASKS} in the rst source; 'wihtout' typo is in the source. Following sentence: 'This can be an indicator of poorly written code that spinloops on a peripheral, or a task that is stuck in an infinite loop.' Note CONFIG_ESP_TASK_WDT_CHECK_IDLE_TASK_CPU1 applies only when not unicore.

document: Using the GNU Compiler Collection (GCC): When is a Volatile Object Accessed?
section: 6.10 When is a Volatile Object Accessed?
verbatim_snippet: C has the concept of volatile objects. These are normally accessed by pointers and used for accessing hardware or inter-thread communication. The standard encourages compilers to refrain from optimizations concerning accesses to volatile objects, but leaves it implementation defined as to what constitutes a volatile access.
notes: The current snippet's 'evaluated strictly according to the rules of the abstract machine' is C-standard wording (ISO C 6.7.3/5.1.2.3), not the GCC manual, and 'compiler may keep a variable in a register' is not in the GCC page. Recommend citing ISO/IEC 9899 for that phrase or using the GCC passage above.
